squeeze/digit: Here is a handwritten seven: twenty eight by twenty eight pixels, so seven hundred and eighty four numbers. Call them x.
squeeze/strokes: Yet a seven is just two pen strokes. Most of those numbers follow from a few facts: where the strokes run, how they slant, how thick the pen was.
squeeze/goal: Can a network learn to describe each digit in far fewer numbers, from the images alone? Alone means without labels: nobody writes down, for each image, which digit it shows.
squeeze/copy: The trick is to ask for a copy. The network takes the image in, and must give the same image back out.
squeeze/wide: If every layer is seven hundred and eighty four wide, that is too easy: it can pass each pixel straight through. A perfect copy, and nothing learned about digits.
squeeze/narrow: So squeeze the middle down to sixteen numbers, and a copy is impossible. To rebuild the digit anyway, those sixteen must keep what matters most: the strokes, their slant, their thickness.
squeeze/neck: That narrow middle is the bottleneck: like the neck of a bottle, it lets only so much through.
halves/enc: The half before the bottleneck is the encoder, an ordinary network: its layers take the seven hundred and eighty four numbers of x to two hundred and fifty six hidden units, then to sixteen.
halves/z: Those sixteen numbers are the code, z: the digit, written in the network's own shorthand.
halves/dec: The other half, the decoder, mirrors it back up to seven hundred and eighty four. Its output is the reconstruction, x hat: the hat marks x as the network rebuilt it.
halves/name: The whole thing is an autoencoder. Auto means self: it encodes its own input, then decodes it back.
halves/ratio: Each number of the code stands in for seven hundred and eighty four over sixteen: forty nine numbers of the input.
halves/shape: Each weight matrix is outputs by inputs, one row per output. So the encoder's first, W one, is two hundred fifty six by seven hundred eighty four.
halves/mirror: The decoder's shapes are the encoder's, flipped: its last, W four, is seven hundred eighty four by two hundred fifty six.
halves/deep: Deep autoencoders were hard to train: from small random weights, almost no gradient reached the early layers.
halves/hinton: In 2006, Geoffrey Hinton and Ruslan Salakhutdinov found a better way to start the weights. Their autoencoder squeezed each digit into thirty numbers, and rebuilt it much better than a widely used method.
loss/loss: To train it, we need a loss, L: one number for how far the output lands from what it should be, which gradient steps push down.
loss/target: And what it should be is the input itself. x is its own target, so no labels are needed.
loss/diff: Take a tiny x: one, zero and two. Say x hat came out as a half, zero and three. Entry by entry, the differences are a half, zero and minus one.
loss/square: Square each, so a miss below costs the same as a miss above, and add: a quarter, plus zero, plus one, is one point two five. That is the squared error.
loss/norm: It is written the norm of x minus x hat, squared. The double bars, read “norm”, give a vector's size as an arrow; squared, that is just this sum of squares.
loss/train: Gradient steps on this loss, back through the decoder and then the encoder, train both halves together, on any pile of images: each is its own target.
